y-m-01-10.title: If you join triangles with matchsticks, how many sticks needed?
y-m-01-10.goal: Find why Seohyeon solution says matchstick count no grow same amount as triangle count grows, and use pattern predict bigger cases.
y-m-01-10.material:
Join triangles in one row with matchsticks. Neighbor triangles share one stick. 1 triangle need 3 sticks, 2 need 5, 3 need 7.
Number of triangles | 1 | 2 | 3
Number of matchsticks | 3 | 5 | 7
Seohyeon wan find how many sticks needed for shape of 5 triangles.
y-m-01-10.thinking.0: Find and fix condition missing in solution
y-m-01-10.thinking.1: Find pattern and use for bigger case
y-m-01-10.prereq.1: Add one at a time and organize in table (Grade 2)
y-m-01-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Seohyeon story wey hard to trust.
y-m-01-10.s.s1.hint.0: For 2 and 3 triangles in table, compare values from Seohyeon method with table.
y-m-01-10.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many new matchsticks you gats put down when you attach one more triangle. 1
y-m-01-10.s.s1.line.0: You need 3 matchsticks to make 1 triangle.
y-m-01-10.s.s1.line.1: 5 triangles need 3 matchsticks five times, so 3×5=15 sticks. 5
y-m-01-10.s.s1.explain: Line 1 correct. For line 2, Seohyeon think each triangle use 3 sticks separately. But neighboring triangles share one, so count separately double count shared stick. Table show 2 triangles need 5, no be 6. So line 2 and 3 both wrong.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.prompt: Find matchstick counts for 4 or more triangles. Pair triangle count k with stick count s, and write 3 ways with different triangle numbers. (k from 4 to 12.)
y-m-01-10.s.s2.hint.0: Check in table how many matchsticks add when triangle count increase by 1.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.hint.1: Find count for 4 triangles, then continue in order.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.ok.c1: Triangle count natural number from 4 to 12.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Choose triangle count as natural number from 4 to 12.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.ok.c2: It be matchstick count fitting table pattern.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.fail.c2: That no be matchstick count for that many triangles. Check how many sticks add each time triangle number increase by 1.
y-m-01-10.s.s2.explain: Each time triangles increase by 1, add 2 sticks. After 3,5,7 come 9,11,13,... So 5 triangles need 11 and 10 triangles need 21. 11 3 5 9
y-m-01-10.s.s3.prompt: How many triangles fit join using all 15 matchsticks?
y-m-01-10.s.s3.hint.0: Increase triangle number one at time, write stick count, and find where 15 appear.
y-m-01-10.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether stick count exactly 15 for triangle number you choose.
y-m-01-10.s.s3.r.a: This idea divide and count matchsticks by 3. Remember neighboring triangles share one stick.
y-m-01-10.s.s3.r.b: You may stop table before it pass 15. Check how many sticks for 6 triangles.
y-m-01-10.s.s3.r.c: This idea continue table pattern to find triangle number making 15 sticks.
y-m-01-10.s.s3.r.d: Check how many sticks for 8 triangles. Is that more than 15?
y-m-01-10.s.s3.explain: Each extra triangle add 2 sticks, so 6 triangles need 13 and 7 need 15. So 15 sticks join 7 triangles.

y-m-01-01.title: How far we fit trust Hajun way to compare sizes?
y-m-01-01.topic: Comparing two-digit numbers (tens place and ones place)
y-m-01-01.goal: Use examples check when di method of deciding di size of two-digit numbers by looking only at di ones digit dey fail, and talk which place to look first when comparing sizes.
y-m-01-01.material: Hajun dey play game where e make two two-digit numbers with number cards and guess which one bigger. For two-digit number, di digit for left na di 'tens place' (how many groups of 10), and di digit for right na di 'ones place' (how many single ones). For example, for 35 di tens digit na 3 and di ones digit na 5. Below na how Hajun explain im method.
y-m-01-01.thinking.0: Decide whether one example wey work enough to trust di whole method
y-m-01-01.thinking.1: Make one case by yourself where di method fail (counterexample)
y-m-01-01.thinking.2: Use place value to decide di order for comparing
y-m-01-01.prereq.0: Reading two-digit number as groups of 10 and single ones (Grade 1, 2nd semester to Grade 2 level)
y-m-01-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose di one line for Hajun story wey hard to trust.
y-m-01-01.s.s1.hint.0: For di two numbers in each line, write how many groups of 10 and how many single ones each one get.
y-m-01-01.s.s1.hint.1: Choose numbers by yourself and count dem with marbles to check whether cases dey where di number with bigger ones digit and di number with bigger tens digit dey opposite.
y-m-01-01.s.s1.line.0: Compare 35 and 32. Di ones digit 5 bigger pass 2, so 35 na di bigger number.
y-m-01-01.s.s1.line.1: Compare 27 and 41. Di ones digit 7 bigger pass 1, so 27 na di bigger number.
y-m-01-01.s.s1.line.2: So for two-digit numbers, di one wey get bigger ones digit na di bigger number.
y-m-01-01.s.s1.explain: Di result for line 1 (35 bigger pass 32) correct. But na only because di tens digits of both numbers na di same, 3, so na di ones digits decide am. For line 2, 27 get 2 groups of 10 and 41 get 4 groups of 10, so 41 na di bigger number. Line 3 dey stretch one example wey work to cover every case. Any line wey you choose, di main thing na to test wetin happen when you look only at di ones digit for two numbers wey get different tens digits.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two different pairs wey Hajun method no work for. Choose two-digit numbers a and b so say a smaller pass b, and di ones digit of a bigger pass di ones digit of b.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a and b wey their tens digits different. How about making di smaller number get plenty ones left?
y-m-01-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write each of di two numbers as groups of 10 and single ones, and check which one really bigger.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Abeg choose a as natural number from 10 to 99.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Abeg choose b as natural number from 10 to 99.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c3: a must be number wey smaller pass b.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.ok.c4: Di ones digit of a bigger. If you use Hajun method, you go wrongly talk say a bigger.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.fail.c4: Di ones digit of a must bigger pass di ones digit of b.
y-m-01-01.s.s2.explain: For example, for 19 and 30, di ones digit 9 bigger pass 0, but 30 get 3 groups of 10, so e bigger pass 19. When di tens digits different, di ones digit no fit decide di size, no matter how big e be. Hajun method fit work only when di tens digits na di same.
y-m-01-01.s.s3.prompt: When you dey compare di sizes of two two-digit numbers, wetin best to look first?
y-m-01-01.s.s3.hint.0: For di two pairs wey you just make, write side by side di order wey you decide by looking only at di ones digit and di real order of which number bigger.
y-m-01-01.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one pair of numbers wey get di same tens digit and one pair wey get different tens digits, then compare which place dey decide di size.
y-m-01-01.s.s3.o.a: Look at di tens digit first, and if dem dey the same, look at di ones digit
y-m-01-01.s.s3.r.a: Di idea be say di number of groups of ten come first, and na only when di number of groups equal di ones dey decide.
y-m-01-01.s.s3.o.b: Add di two digits of each number and choose di one wey get bigger sum
y-m-01-01.s.s3.r.b: Di sum of di digits fit different from di size of di number. Compare 19 (1 and 9) and 30 (3 and 0).
y-m-01-01.s.s3.o.c: Di result na di same, no matter which digit you look first
y-m-01-01.s.s3.r.c: Di result fit change depending on which place you look first. Compare di results of di two methods for 27 and 41.
y-m-01-01.s.s3.o.d: Look at di ones digit first, and if dem dey the same, look at di tens digit
y-m-01-01.s.s3.r.d: Check wetin happen if you use dis order for di examples wey you just make. When di tens digits different, di ones digit no fit decide which one bigger.
y-m-01-01.s.s3.explain: For two-digit numbers, di one wey get more groups of 10 na di bigger number. Na only when di number of groups equal, single ones dey decide. Na why we dey look at tens place first.

y-m-01-03.title: Four Friends' Calculation Methods: We Fit Trust All of Dem?
y-m-01-03.topic: Compare addition methods for two-digit numbers (make 10, split apart)
y-m-01-03.goal: Sort which methods for adding 38 and 27 correct or wrong, make pairs of ones digits that make 10, and explain why that method handy.
y-m-01-03.material:
One bag get 38 marbles and another 27. Four friends use different methods to find total when both bags gather together.
- Ayun: I take 2 from 27 so 38 become 40. 40+25=65.
- Doyun: I join 3 tens and 2 tens, and 8 ones and 7 ones separately. 50+15=65.
- Seojin: 3+2=5, and 8+7=15, so I write 5 and 15 side by side and say 515.
- Harin: I treat 27 as 30. 38+30=68, then subtract 3 I add, answer 65.
y-m-01-03.thinking.0: Compare different methods and judge right/wrong
y-m-01-03.thinking.1: Make different pairs meeting a condition
y-m-01-03.prereq.0: Split two-digit number into tens bundles and single ones (Grade 2 level) 10
y-m-01-03.prereq.1: Know 10 single ones make one ten bundle 10
y-m-01-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all suitable methods for adding 38 and 27.
y-m-01-03.s.s1.hint.0: Find how each friend change 38 or 27; check if total marbles stay same.
y-m-01-03.s.s1.hint.1: Picture marbles in bundles of 10 and check how many marbles each friend calculation make.
y-m-01-03.s.s1.o.a: Seojin: write 5 and 15 side-by-side to get 515
y-m-01-03.s.s1.r.a: 5 and 15 no be tens bundles and ones. 3 bundles and 2 bundles na 5 bundles; 15 ones na 1 bundle and 5 ones. Look at how dem join these.
y-m-01-03.s.s1.o.b: Ayun: move 2 from 27, then add 40 and 25
y-m-01-03.s.s1.r.b: This use fact total stay same even if you move some.
y-m-01-03.s.s1.o.c: Harin: treat 27 as 30, add, then subtract 3 again
y-m-01-03.s.s1.r.c: This use idea of returning the extra amount you count.
y-m-01-03.s.s1.o.d: Doyun: add bundles separately and ones separately, then join at end
y-m-01-03.s.s1.r.d: Gather tens and ones separately, then put dem together. 10
y-m-01-03.s.s1.explain: Ayun use fact total stay same even if 2 move; Harin return 3 extra at end; Doyun gather bundles and ones separately. All give 65. Seojin miss say 15 include one ten bundle. 5 bundles plus 15 ones na 6 bundles and 5 ones, so 65. 10
y-m-01-03.s.s2.prompt: Find pairs of two-digit numbers where Ayun method (take from one to make exact ten) convenient. For numbers a,b, ones digits together gats make exactly 10, sum no pass 100. Same pair in reverse order count once. 10
y-m-01-03.s.s2.hint.0: Choose only ones digits first, then choose tens digits.
y-m-01-03.s.s2.hint.1: Move from one number to make ten bundle exact, like Ayun with your pair, and check total. 10
y-m-01-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Choose a as natural number from 10 to 89.
y-m-01-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Choose b as natural number from 10 to 89.
y-m-01-03.s.s2.ok.c4: Sum of two numbers no pass 100.
y-m-01-03.s.s2.explain: For example, for 24 and 46, 4 ones and 6 ones meet and make one exact 10 bundle, so sum 70 with no ones left. 38 and 12 make 50 too. Pairs where ones disappear easy to calculate.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.prompt: Why pairs you make easy to calculate with Ayun method?
y-m-01-03.s.s3.hint.0: Lay your pairs out and check wetin same for all.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write separately wetin vary by pair (even/odd, tens digit) and wetin same in all.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.r.a: Odd pairs dey too, like 15 and 75. Whether a number even no connect to this method.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.o.b: Because tens digits of two numbers same
y-m-01-03.s.s3.r.b: Look your pairs. Some get different tens digits, like 24 and 46.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.o.c: Because numbers small, any method easy
y-m-01-03.s.s3.r.c: This idea look only at number size, no check if method especially handy for pair.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.o.d: Because gathering ones make exactly one bundle of ten
y-m-01-03.s.s3.r.d: This idea point out ones fill ten bundle and turn into number of tens.
y-m-01-03.s.s3.explain: When ones join, dem make exactly 10, so new bundle form and 0 ones remain. You only count bundles. 10

y-m-01-06.title: Making three-digit numbers with number cards 0, 4, and 7
y-m-01-06.topic: Place value and 0 (making three-digit numbers with number cards)
y-m-01-06.goal: Understand say when you make numbers with number cards, putting 0 for di very front no dey make three-digit number; make plenty three-digit numbers wey fit one condition, and judge how di possible numbers dey change when di cards change.
y-m-01-06.material: You get one each of number cards 0, 4, and 7. You wan make one three-digit number using every card once. Two friends wey make di smallest number give different answers. Mina talk 047, and Jiu talk 407.
y-m-01-06.thinking.0: Find di problem with one method wey look correct
y-m-01-06.thinking.1: Make plenty numbers wey fit one condition
y-m-01-06.thinking.2: Think whether di possible cases dey change when di cards change

y-m-01-06.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think about Mina answer and Jiu answer?
y-m-01-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write 047, 074, and 407 based on how many 100s, 10s, and 1s dey inside dem.
y-m-01-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how many 100s dey inside one number when di hundreds digit na 0.
y-m-01-06.s.s1.o.a: Jiu correct. 047 na di same as 47, so e no be three-digit number.
y-m-01-06.s.s1.r.a: Dis idea notice say di 0 for di very front only dey occupy one place, and not even one group of 100 dey.

y-m-01-06.s.s1.r.b: Dis idea judge by looking only di size of each single digit. Think wetin you get when you read 047.
y-m-01-06.s.s1.o.c: Both correct. E depend on how you read am.
y-m-01-06.s.s1.r.c: Di size of number no dey change according to how you read am. Look how many groups of 10 and groups of 100 dey inside 047 and 407.

y-m-01-06.s.s1.r.d: 074 too get 0 for di very front. Think how e different from 74.
y-m-01-06.s.s1.explain: Di hundreds digit for 047 na 0, so e no get even one group of 100. So e na di same as 47 and e be two-digit number. Three-digit number must get digit wey no be 0 for hundreds place, so di smallest three-digit number wey you fit make with cards 0, 4, and 7 na 407.
y-m-01-06.s.s2.prompt: Among di three-digit numbers wey you make using each of cards 0, 4, and 7 once, find three different numbers wey bigger pass 450. Enter di hundreds digit a, tens digit b, and ones digit c.

y-m-01-06.s.s2.fail.c3: If di hundreds digit na 0, e no be three-digit number.
y-m-01-06.s.s2.fail.c4: Di number wey you make no bigger pass 450.
y-m-01-06.s.s2.explain: Di three-digit numbers wey you fit make with cards 0, 4, and 7 na four: 407, 470, 704, and 740. Among dem, three numbers bigger pass 450: 470, 704, and 740. 407 smaller pass 450, so e no enter.
y-m-01-06.s.s3.prompt: If di cards na 0, 0, and 7, how many three-digit numbers you fit make using all three cards?
y-m-01-06.s.s3.hint.0: First decide which card fit go for hundreds place.
y-m-01-06.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether di number dey change when you swap di other two cards.

y-m-01-06.s.s3.r.c: Maybe you judge without testing whether you fit put 7 for hundreds place.
y-m-01-06.s.s3.r.d: 070 get 0 for hundreds place, so e na di same as 70. Check whether na really three-digit number.
y-m-01-06.s.s3.explain: 7 must dey for hundreds place, and di two remaining 0 cards go still make di same 700 even if you swap their order. So na only one, 700, you fit make. If di cards dey the same, swapping their order dey give di same number.

y-m-01-02.title: Wetin happen when you join one odd number and one odd number?
y-m-01-02.topic: Sum of odd and even numbers (trying to pair dem up)
y-m-01-02.goal: See how confidence dey change when examples increase and when you learn di reason, and follow di idea wey use pairing explain why joining two odd numbers dey give even number.
y-m-01-02.material: When you pair marbles two by two, if one remain, di number of marbles na 'odd'; if none remain, e na 'even'. 3 na one pair and one remain, so e odd; 8 na four pairs, so e even. Seoa wan find out whether joining one odd number of marbles and another odd number together for one place go give odd or even number of marbles altogether.
y-m-01-02.thinking.0: Notice di difference for confidence between one example and plenty examples
y-m-01-02.thinking.1: Check say knowing di reason dey let you continue your thinking to new cases
y-m-01-02.thinking.2: Make several pairs wey get one given sum
y-m-01-02.prereq.0: Trying to pair things two by two (Grade 1 to 2 level)
y-m-01-02.prereq.1: Di meaning of odd and even (whether anything remain or not)
y-m-01-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose how your thinking dey change each time new information come up.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each step, first decide your thought with one sentence, then compare whether di new information dey make dat thought stronger or dey shake am.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.hint.1: Tell di difference between whether wetin come up na 'example' or 'reason', and think about which one change your confidence more.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Seoa put 3 marbles and 5 marbles together for one place and get 8. 8 na even number.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin you think about di idea 'joining one odd number and one odd number dey give even number'?
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.after: One example dey help you form guess, but e no dey guarantee every case. Test am more with other odd numbers.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: E look like say joining odd numbers dey give odd number
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Di result of joining 3 and 5, 8, na even number. Dis idea no fit dat example.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Now I sure say e always even
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Dis idea dey promise every case from one example. Look back whether you test other odd numbers too.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Na only one example dey, so I wan check other odd numbers too
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Dis idea understand say one example no fit tell you whether e always so.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: E look like say e go be even, but I never sure yet
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Dis idea dey make guess but e hold back from being sure.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Seoa tried more cases: 1 and 1 make 2, 7 and 9 make 16, 11 and 13 make 24, and 21 and 35 make 56. All even.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.after: When many examples work, you believe more. But you no fit try every odd number, so next step na know why.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: I no fit believe just because few examples work
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This idea no value power of collecting examples enough. When examples work, belief fit grow.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Putting odd numbers together sometimes give even number, sometimes odd
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Among examples we test, odd number no become even even once.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Many examples work, so my belief say e always even don grow
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: Examples plenty and belief grow. But untested cases still dey.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: I never test every case, so I wan know the reason
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This idea see say even with many examples, confidence get limit if you no know reason.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Seoa find reason. If you pair odd number of marbles two by two, one remain. If you join two piles wey each get odd number, the two leftover marbles form pair. (3 na ○○ ○ and 5 na ○○ ○○ ○, so one remain at end.)
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: This explanation fit work for plenty marbles (101 and 203)?
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Explanation use only point say "one remain when pair two by two," whatever number of marbles, so e work for big numbers too.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: E only work for small numbers; for big ones you gats join dem and find out
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Think whether explanation change with marble number. Check if leftover count stay same as numbers grow.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: With big numbers, more than one marble fit remain
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: When you pair two by two, leftover na either 0 or 1. E no change as numbers grow.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: This explanation no tell us anything
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This idea give up judging without thinking when explanation apply.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Always one marble remain, so e fit work for big numbers too
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This idea rely on reason "one remain each time," no be number size.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.info: Seoa join three odd piles (3,5,7), get 15. 15 odd. 3 5
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.ask: Wetin happen when you join three odd piles? How you fit use earlier idea?
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.after: If 3 marbles remain, 2 pair and 1 left. So total odd. If you know why, you fit predict new cases without gather examples.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.o.a: Earlier odd numbers together give even, so this time e look like e go be even too
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.r.a: This idea carry result for two piles straight to three. Count how many leftover marbles dey.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.o.b: E look like e always go be odd, however many piles dey
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.r.b: With two piles result even. Check if result fit change depending how many piles.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.o.c: Two piles make even number, so add one more pile and e go odd
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.r.c: This idea continue using earlier reason for new case.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.o.d: I only fit know by trying more examples
y-m-01-02.s.s1.st.3.r.d: Trying more examples good too. Also think if reason let you guess without testing examples.
y-m-01-02.s.s1.reflect: At first I guess from one example, my confidence grow as examples increase, and when I know reason, I fit talk about very big numbers too. Knowing why let me extend thinking to new case (three piles). Say which step make confidence firm and wetin cause am.
y-m-01-02.s.s2.prompt: Find three different pairs of odd numbers wey sum to 20. Call smaller a and larger b.
y-m-01-02.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether once you choose one number, the other automatically set.

y-m-01-11.title: When you add the two digits of 9 times table, always get 9?
y-m-01-11.topic: Digit pattern in 9 times table (how far e hold?)
y-m-01-11.goal: While checking pattern with many examples, meet a place where e break, judge what range pattern gats apply to, and find breaking example yourself.
y-m-01-11.material: Sua memorize 9 times table and notice something strange. For 9×2=18, digits 1 and 8; for 9×3=27, digits 2 and 7; for 9×4=36, digits 3 and 6; each pair add to 9. Sua wan test pattern more.

y-m-01-11.thinking.1: Find breaking example and restate range
y-m-01-11.prereq.1: Know tens and ones digits of two-digit number
y-m-01-11.s.s1.prompt: Choose your thinking each time new info come.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write range of products checked so far in one line and see whether pattern checked only within that range.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.hint.1: For every new product, add two digits yourself and check pattern.

y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin you think di digits of 9×5 go add up to? Predict before you calculate.

y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: I think e go be 9. All di examples before na
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Dis na guess wey carry di pattern of earlier examples straight go di next one.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I think e go be smaller than 9
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Check whether any sign show say di sum dey get smaller for earlier examples.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I fit only know if I multiply am by myself
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Checking am by yourself na reasonable way too. Predict and check together make you test pattern better.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.info: Sua check all of 9×5=45, 9×6=54, 9×7=63, 9×8=72, and 9×9=81. For all of dem, di sum of di digits na 9.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: Di digits of 9×10, 9×11, ... go add up to 9 too? Wetin you think now?
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.after: All 9 inside di multiplication table dey correct, so di pattern believable. But dem never test di products from 9×10 go front.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.o.a: For 9 times table, di sum of di two digits always na 9, even from now
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Dis idea carry di fact say all 9 inside di multiplication table correct go beyond di table at once.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.o.b: E correct inside di multiplication table, and I wan check beyond am by myself
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Dis idea separate di range wey correct from di range wey dem never try.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Beyond di multiplication table no be 9 times table, so e no matter
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.r.c: 9×10 too na number wey be some multiple of 9. E hard to talk say e no be 9 times table just because e dey beyond di multiplication table.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.o.d: All 9 inside di times table correct, so e sure without more checking
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Just because 9 correct, e hard to talk say e certain for products wey you never try. Some products still remain to check.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.info: Sua try more. 9×10=90, and 9 plus 0 make 9. 9×11=99, and 9 plus 9 make 18. 9×12=108, and 1 plus 0 plus 8 make 9.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: Di pattern no hold for 9×11. How we fit state di pattern again?
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.after: If even one, like 99, no fit, you no fit talk say '9 times table always'. But e correct up to 9×9, so you fit make di range smaller and talk say 'inside di multiplication table'.

y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: 99 no be 9 added 11 times, na di exact product of 9×11. Check di calculation again.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Di pattern correct up to 9×9, and e fit no correct beyond dat
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Dis idea make di range wey correct smaller and state am again.

y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Dis pattern no useful. Make dem throw am away
y-m-01-11.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Di fact say e correct inside multiplication table still dey. Think di range wey you fit use am.
y-m-01-11.s.s1.reflect: When di first examples correct, confidence for di pattern grow, but some range never test yet. When di pattern break for 9×11, 'always' gatz change to 'inside di multiplication table'. Talk which step make your confidence grow and which step make di range smaller.

y-m-01-11.s.s3.explain: From 9×2 to 9×9 di sum of di two digits na 9, and some products like 9×11=99 get sum of 18 too. Pattern dey correct when you state di range wey e right together with am.
